questions.stem: The centre of gravity of a uniform metre rule is located at the

options.text: 0 cm mark
25 cm mark
50 cm mark
100 cm mark

questions.explanation: Uniform means the mass is spread evenly along the rule, so the two halves have identical weight and the whole weight acts at the geometric centre — the 50 cm mark. This is why a uniform rule pivoted at 50 cm balances with nothing on it.

distractorRationale.a: This is one end of the rule; the weight of the other 100 cm would give a large unbalanced moment there
distractorRationale.b: The quarter point would only be the CG if the rule were much heavier on one side
distractorRationale.d: This is the far end, again not a point of balance

questions.stem: The centre of gravity of a body is the point at which

options.text: the whole weight of the body appears to act
the body is thickest
all the external forces on the body are applied
the body has the greatest density

questions.explanation: The weight of a body is really spread across every particle in it, but for calculating moments and equilibrium the whole weight can be replaced by a single force acting at one point. That point is the centre of gravity.

distractorRationale.b: Thickness is not the same as weight distribution; a thick but hollow section may be light
distractorRationale.c: External forces such as tensions and reactions act wherever they are applied, not at the CG
distractorRationale.d: Density varies through a body and the CG depends on how the whole mass is distributed, not on a single densest point

questions.stem: The centre of gravity of an irregular cardboard lamina is best found by

options.text: weighing the lamina on a beam balance
suspending it freely from three different points and using a plumb line each time
measuring its longest dimension and halving it
floating it on water and marking the waterline

questions.explanation: A body suspended freely always settles with its centre of gravity vertically below the point of suspension, because otherwise the weight would exert a turning moment. Drawing that vertical line from three separate suspension points gives three lines whose intersection is the centre of gravity.

distractorRationale.a: Weighing gives the total weight but tells you nothing about where it acts
distractorRationale.c: Halving a dimension only locates the CG for a symmetrical shape, and an irregular lamina is not symmetrical
distractorRationale.d: The waterline depends on density and shape and does not mark the CG

questions.stem: A body is in stable equilibrium. When it is displaced slightly, its centre of gravity

options.text: falls, and the body topples over
rises, and the body returns to its original position
stays at the same height, and the body rests in its new position
moves outside the body

questions.explanation: Raising the centre of gravity means work has been done against gravity, so the body has gained potential energy. Gravity then acts to restore the lowest-energy position, which brings the body back — the defining behaviour of stable equilibrium.

distractorRationale.a: A falling CG describes unstable equilibrium, where the body topples further
distractorRationale.c: An unchanged CG height describes neutral equilibrium, as for a ball on a level table
distractorRationale.d: Where the CG lies relative to the material is a matter of shape and has nothing to do with stability

questions.stem: The stability of a body is increased by

options.text: raising its centre of gravity and narrowing its base
lowering its centre of gravity and widening its base
raising its centre of gravity and widening its base
reducing its total weight only

questions.explanation: A body topples once the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base. A low centre of gravity and a wide base both mean the body must be tilted through a much larger angle before that happens. This is why a Bunsen burner has a heavy base and racing cars are built low and wide.

distractorRationale.a: Both changes reduce stability — this describes a top-heavy object on a narrow foot
distractorRationale.c: Widening the base helps, but raising the CG works against it
distractorRationale.d: Weight alone does not decide stability; a light but top-heavy object topples easily

questions.stem: The centre of gravity of a uniform triangular lamina lies

options.text: at the midpoint of the longest side
at the vertex opposite the longest side
at the point where the three medians intersect
outside the lamina

questions.explanation: For a uniform triangular lamina the centre of gravity is the centroid, the point where the three medians meet. It lies two-thirds of the way along each median measured from the vertex, and it is always inside the triangle.

distractorRationale.a: A side's midpoint is on the boundary, so the material on the far side would produce an unbalanced moment
distractorRationale.b: A vertex has almost no surrounding material, so it cannot be the balance point
distractorRationale.d: For a triangle the centroid always lies inside; only shapes like rings or crescents have an external CG

questions.stem: The centre of gravity of a body must always lie within the material of that body.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. For a circular ring, a horseshoe or a boomerang, the centre of gravity lies in the empty space enclosed by the material. The centre of gravity marks where the total weight effectively acts, which need not coincide with any actual particle of the body.

questions.stem: A double-decker bus is more likely to overturn on a sharp bend when passengers are seated upstairs rather than downstairs because

options.text: the total weight of the bus increases
the centre of gravity of the bus is raised
the base of the bus becomes narrower
the tyres lose grip on the road

questions.explanation: The same passengers sitting higher up shift the combined centre of gravity upwards. With a higher centre of gravity, a smaller angle of tilt is enough to bring the vertical line through the CG outside the wheelbase, so the bus overturns more readily.

distractorRationale.a: The total weight is the same wherever the passengers sit, so weight alone cannot be the reason
distractorRationale.c: The wheelbase is fixed by the vehicle's construction and does not change with seating
distractorRationale.d: Grip depends on tyres, road surface and speed, none of which change when passengers move upstairs

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 1.0 m and weight 20 N has a weight of 30 N firmly fixed at one end. Calculate the distance of the centre of gravity of the whole system from that loaded end. Give your answer in metres.
questions.explanation: The rod's own weight acts at its midpoint, 0.50 m from the loaded end, and the 30 N weight is at that end so its distance is zero. Taking moments about the loaded end: $(20 + 30)\bar{x} = (20 \times 0.50) + (30 \times 0) = 10\ \text{N m}$, so $\bar{x} = \frac{10}{50} = 0.20\ \text{m}$. The centre of gravity has shifted from the middle towards the heavier end, as expected.

questions.stem: A solid sphere rests on a smooth horizontal table. When it is rolled slightly and released it stays in its new position. The sphere is in

options.text: stable equilibrium
unstable equilibrium
neutral equilibrium
no equilibrium at all

questions.explanation: The centre of a sphere always stays one radius above the table however far it rolls, so its centre of gravity neither rises nor falls. With no change in potential energy there is no restoring or overturning moment, which is exactly neutral equilibrium.

distractorRationale.a: Stable equilibrium would require the CG to rise on displacement so the sphere rolled back to where it started
distractorRationale.b: Unstable equilibrium would require the CG to fall, sending the body further away on its own
distractorRationale.d: The sphere is at rest with zero resultant force and zero net moment, so it is certainly in equilibrium
